method: Complete candidate survey followed by individual editorial choices and written reasons, applied to the existing complete guide to keep it within 300 quotations. All verified authorized selections included. Priority given to foundational teachings, substantive explanations, necessary qualifications, distinctive applications, narrative examples and thematic breadth across hope that deepens life, images at the edge of understanding, the soul and its earthly instrument, eternal life, progress through justice and mercy, recognition and spiritual influence, prayer and deeds across separation, consolation amid grief, lives remembered through service, faithfulness under persecution, welcome and reunion, and the return to the work of life. Neither citation count nor source order used as a ranking rule. Imported wording checked separately; version differences remain explicit. The existing reading arc is retained.

selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that whatsoever a man sows here he reaps there; a memorable statement of continuity between conduct and the life beyond.

selected.text: All living beings in that City are unaware of death, and death never overtakes them.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that the living beings of the City are unaware of death; retains the dialogue named in its group’s why.

selected.text: Q. Is a soul ever annihilated? … A. No. It will be placed in different conditions by God's Mercy, and will eventually progress
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that no soul is annihilated but each will be placed in different conditions by God’s mercy and will eventually progress; a brief, hopeful qualification.

selected.text: They, who have passed into the Divine Garden, pray for us there, as we pray for them here
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that those who have passed into the Divine Garden pray for us as we pray for them; a concise statement of mutual prayer.

selected.text: If both had the same degree of development, they would be re-united immediately after death.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that two souls of the same degree of development would be reunited immediately after death; a concise condition for reunion.

selected.text: Moral life consists in the government of one's self. Immortality is government of a human soul by the Divine Will.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that immortality is the government of the soul by the Divine Will; a distinctive definition linking eternal life to character.

selected.text: In the Gospel (St. Luke 12:4) it is said: "Be not afraid of them that kill the body and after that have no more that they can do. But I will tell you whom ye shall fear. Fear him which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell. Yea, I may unto you, fear him." … 'Abdu'l-Baha said that this means that the death of the body is of no importance and not in the least to be feared, because a spiritual soul lives forever. But the thing to be feared is the death of the spirit
selected.reason: Reported interpretation by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá of Luke 12:4 that bodily death is not to be feared but the death of the spirit is; connects the subject to Gospel teaching.

selected.text: the prophets of God forfeited this world, renounced everything material and gave their hearts to the heavenly world. Were there nothing after death, Christ would not have accepted the cross; the prophets of all time would not have sacrificed their lives. They were in touch with the celestial world and they overlooked this transitory life
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that were there nothing after death Christ would not have accepted the cross nor the prophets sacrificed their lives; a distinctive argument from sacrifice.

selected.text: I swear by the Educator of existence that the life of this world is death and its comfort is affliction, but as long as the veil remains, man is not aware of the harshness and constriction of this world. When the veil is lifted through ascension to the Kingdom of bounty, one realizes that this world was like a woman's womb and this space a narrow prison of trials
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá swearing that the life of this world is death and its comfort affliction, unrecognized until the veil is lifted at ascension; a strong statement of perspective.

selected.text: Consider how a being, in the world of the womb, was deaf of ear and blind of eye, and mute of tongue; how he was bereft of any perceptions at all. But once, out of that world of darkness, he passed into this world of light, then his eye saw, his ear heard, his tongue spoke. In the same way, once he hath hastened away from this mortal place into the Kingdom of God, then he will be born in the spirit; then the eye of his perception will open, the ear of his soul will hearken, and all the truths of which he was ignorant before will be made plain and clear.
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: This is why in the holy books it is mentioned that after the ascension of a soul, good deeds and charitable works should be performed for that soul, and these good deeds and charitable works become the cause of the elevation of its station. Thus it becomes clear that progress for man--meaning the acquisition of divine perfections and infinite bounties--is possible in every world. However, man's appearance in this world is for progress in both stations and perfections, while in the next world progress is confined to divine perfections.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explaining that good deeds and charitable works performed for a departed soul elevate its station, and that progress in the next world is in perfections; a foundational statement on charity for the dead.

selected.text: Taking the material ocean as an illustration, 'Abduil-Baha said, The atoms composing an ocean are, in appearance the ocean, but the identity of the atoms remains. So it is with our individuality in the ocean of life
selected.reason: Reported illustration by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that atoms keep their identity within the ocean, as individuality does in the ocean of life; supplies the ocean image of individuality.

selected.text: It is even possible for those who have died in sin and unbelief to be transformed, that is, to become the object of divine forgiveness. This is through the grace of God and not through His justice, for grace is to bestow without desert and justice is to give that which is deserved.
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Those souls for whom the spiritual life has been perfected shall never perish or cease to exist. They derived benefits from this life and bore fruit. How wondrous is that fruit! It is nearness to God; it is eternal life; it is everlasting illumination; it is unchanging existence; it is a life shining with light and the other human perfections, even while on this speck of dust.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that souls whose spiritual life is perfected bear the fruit of nearness to God and eternal life even on this earth; joins continuing existence to spiritual awakening.

selected.text: And the answer to the fourth question: the center of the Sun of Truth is in the supernal world---the Kingdom of God. Those souls who are pure and unsullied, upon the dissolution of their elemental frames, hasten away to the world of God, and that world is within this world. The people of this world, however, are unaware of that world, and are even as the mineral and the vegetable that know nothing of the world of the animal
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Question: Is individuality retained by various individual consciousnesses? … Abdu'l Baha: Complete individuality belongs only to the station of the Prophet. Those who follow him are under the "shadow" of his station. After death man does not develop through conscious effort, but through the power of Divine Bounty or unfoldment. All good works, loving memories, prayers and help from lesser beings assist the soul to push forward after death
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on individuality and the Prophet’s station, adding that good works, loving memories and prayers assist the soul after death; the distinctive claim named in its group’s why.

selected.text: Thou hast written that some of the friends have informed thee that if man does not progress, he will perish and become nonexistent. What is intended is not absolute nonexistence. The meaning is that the existence of a heedless person in comparison to the existence of a perfect individual is like being nonexistent. For instance, a stone is nonexistent in comparison to man, even though it existeth in the mineral condition. In brief, all souls exist, but the existence of the heedless and the ignorant in comparison to the existence of the perfect and the wise is like nonexistence. A detailed explanation of this question was given to Miss Barney, and no doubt thou shalt obtain a copy. The intention of this discourse is that both the ignorant and the wise possess existence, but the existence of the ignorant is like that of a stone, while the existence of the perfect individual resembleth
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá correcting the idea that heedless souls become nonexistent, explaining that their existence is like a stone’s beside a perfect person’s; a clear correction of absolute annihilation.

selected.text: The world of existence is like an ocean and these determined beings are its waves. Although they have existence and visibility, they are considered non-existent and lost, except for the sacred realities of divine souls. Although they too are determined beings, yet being illumined from the praised station and assisted from the extended shadow, they attain eternal realization in the world of existence and find everlasting determination. This is the meaning of "All things perish save His face."
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s image of existence as an ocean whose waves are counted lost save for divine souls who attain eternal realization; supplies the ocean image the questions mention.

selected.text: All realities and souls are immortal, even the souls of unbelievers and defective souls, but in relation to the souls of the holy ones and sanctified souls, the former have no importance and significance. This piece of wood, for instance, exists, but in relation to the existence of man its existence is insignificant. As for the immortality of heedless souls after relinquishing the elemental body, their immortality is the same as extinction because they are deprived of a goodly life. Consider the mineral. Although it continues to exist in the plane of the mineral, in comparison to the existence of man it is pure nonexistence. The other worlds are habitations for the improvement of realities, the transformation of essences, and the renewal of character, but the elevation of ranks and obtaining forgiveness and pardon is another matter
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that all souls are immortal but the heedless are as nonexistent beside the holy, with the other worlds offering elevation and pardon; a substantive answer from Dublin.

selected.text: The Master gave this explanation of the passage, "Let the dead bury the dead": … "Dust has existence, the body of man has existence, but when the body of man is non-existent it returns to dust; therefore, dust in its relation to the body of man is non-existent, but in its own station it has existence. The dead are in the station of dust. They both have life, but what a difference
selected.reason: Reported explanation by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá of “Let the dead bury the dead” through the comparison of dust and the human body; interprets a Gospel image of spiritual death.

selected.text: in the spiritual world and divine Kingdom there is no time and place, since times and limits are relative matters, like east and west, south and north, night and day, month and year - these all are relative to the earth, not the celestial sun
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that the spiritual world has no time and place, since such limits are relative to the earth; a clear qualification of how the next world may be pictured.

selected.text: Q. If one refuses the Cause of Baha'u'llah during his lifetime, may he hear of it after death? … A. Yes, he will hear of it in his next life, but through the mercy of God, not through his own ability
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that one who refused the Cause in life may hear of it after death through God’s mercy; addresses those without recognition.

selected.text: Q. Do we have to leave the body in order to return to God, or is the true return when the Word becomes Spirit in the heart and ascends as sweet incense back to God? … A. This is right, this is right
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá affirming that the true return to God is when the Word becomes Spirit in the heart; a distinctive turn from death to present transformation.

selected.text: Q. What is the connection of the spirit with the body? … A. It has the same connection as the sun has with the mirror. Death is the name for the dissolution of this connection
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that the spirit is connected to the body as the sun to a mirror and that death is the dissolution of this connection; introduces the guide’s mirror image.

selected.text: Spirit is the highest and supreme development of the soul. Soul is the material or outer self--the Mind. is the action of the Soul's powers. The Body is the physical covering or medium in which Mind acts and functions. At death everything but Spirit is destroyed and becomes extinct.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá defining spirit, soul, mind and body and saying all but spirit is destroyed at death; keeps a distinct vocabulary named in its group’s why.

selected.text: Asked if disembodied souls could communicate with embodied ones, He replied: … "Yes, but they do not do it through medums nor in material ways, but in spiritual ways
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that disembodied souls communicate with the embodied in spiritual ways, not through mediums; complements the caution about material phenomena.

selected.text: Q. What becomes of an undeveloped infant's soul? … A. It rests with the mercy of God and through the eternal bounty it will not be deprived of that mercy
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that an undeveloped infant’s soul rests with the mercy of God; addresses children as the group’s why describes.

selected.text: The question was asked if it were possible to establish communication with the dead, and whether it was wise or advisable to attend seances or to engage in table-turning, spirit-rapping, etc.] … The Master said these rappings, etc., were all material things, and of the body. What is needed is to rise above the material to the realms of the purely Spiritual. Table-turning and such like were material, a natural result, and not spiritual. … But it was possible to communicate with the dead through the condition of the character and the heart
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that séances and table-turning are material, while communication with the dead is through the condition of character and heart; the guide’s caution about material phenomena.

selected.text: Shall I find my mother again?" … The Master said: "Certainly. Separation is only in the world of bodies
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá to a questioner asking whether she will find her mother again, that separation is only in the world of bodies; an intimate promise of reunion.

selected.text: Supreme importance should be attached, therefore, not to this first creation but rather to the future life.
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Why should you wish to return here? In My Father's House are many mansions -- many, many worlds! Why should you desire to come back to this particular planet
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asking why anyone would wish to return to this planet when there are many mansions and many worlds; a vivid answer to reincarnation.

selected.text: This lesson is to explain, if it be possible for either a believer or an unbeliever to advance in the next world. … The believer attains to eternal life in this world, but the unbeliever is eternally veiled from the presence of God. Eternal life is knowledge of God and eternal punishment is deprivation of the Sight of God. According to the statements in the Gospel, those who do not believe are eternally condemned, while those who … are believers will be in eternal joy and happiness. But the Mercy of God surpasses His Condemnation
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá defining eternal life as knowledge of God and punishment as deprivation of His sight, adding that God’s mercy surpasses His condemnation; a substantive teaching.

selected.text: Question: Is there any predominant quality which man should develop in order to obtain especial excellence or power after death? … Answer: No, man should develop all his qualities for each quality has its own use and function
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that no single quality should be developed for the next life, since each quality has its own use; a distinctive practical counsel on preparation.

selected.text: Our real gathering is There! Our divine Assembly is There! Our spiritual Feast is There! Our eternal union is There
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá to Zoroastrian pilgrims that our real gathering, feast and eternal union are There; a concise statement of companionship.

selected.text: when the birds of paradise soar to the holy gardens it is cause for joy, not mourning, and occasion for gladness, not regret.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying that the flight of the birds of paradise to the holy gardens is cause for joy, not mourning; the counsel named in its group’s why.

selected.text: And he says fear God and dread Azrael, for soon breaths will be cut off and we will hasten to that other world and find each other
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s family letter relaying a playful warning to fear God and Azrael before we find each other in the other world; the exchange named in its group’s why.

selected.text: Although she passed away from this material world, she is living in her spiritual children
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying a departed woman lives in her spiritual children; a concise statement of legacy.

selected.text: She verily ascended to God and returned to Him just as she had appeared from Him. She hath returned, rested, rejoiced and is overjoyed.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying a departed woman returned to God as she had appeared from Him, rested and rejoiced; a brief statement of return.

selected.text: The divine worlds are limitless, and the rewards for goodly deeds and spiritual qualities lie hidden and treasured in all these worlds.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh stating that the divine worlds are limitless and that the rewards of goodly deeds lie treasured in all of them; a concise statement of reward.

selected.text: Thy death was naught but a translation from the earthly abode to the divine dwelling, from the lowest station to the Most Exalted Companion
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh calling death naught but a translation from the earthly abode to the divine dwelling; a concise authoritative definition.

selected.text: You have not lost him. At most, there is now a temporary separation between you. In the Kingdom there will be a meeting. It is precisely like taking a journey. You will meet
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that the bereaved listener has not lost him, the separation being temporary and like a journey; a plain promise of meeting.

selected.text: For some time I have been ill and weary of life in this world, yearning to journey in the other world. If I depart from this nest and hasten to the realm of the Kingdom, do not forget me, do not remain silent, do not seek rest. Remember my counsels, heed my advice. … Act in such wise that you may shine forth in the Kingdom of God and adorn your countenance with the light of Baha and the radiance of the Covenant. Physical splendor lasteth but a moment, and the ocean of joy in this earthly realm is but a dewdrop. Show forth a lofty aspiration and be not content with a moment or a dewdrop. … I shall not forget thee, neither in this world nor in the world to come
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, ill and yearning for the next world, asking His friends not to forget Him but to heed His counsels, and promising not to forget them; links remembrance with carrying forward counsel.

selected.text: To consider that after the death of the body the spirit perishes, is like imagining that a bird in a cage will be destroyed if the cage is broken--though the bird has nothing to fear from the destruction of the cage. Our body is like the cage, and the spirit is like the bird. We see that without the cage this bird flies in the world of sleep; therefore, if the cage becomes broken, the bird will continue to exist; its feelings will be even more powerful, its perceptions greater and its happiness increased. In truth, from hell it reaches a paradise of delights, because for the thankful bird there is no paradise greater than freedom from the cage.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s image of the body as a cage and the spirit as a bird whose perceptions and happiness increase when the cage is broken; one of the guide’s central images.

selected.text: Immortal existence in the beyond is but a continuation of our life and work here, through other means, in other forms, in other surroundings.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that immortal existence is a continuation of our life and work here in other forms; joins the next life to present work.

selected.text: Q. Are we not able, through love and faith, to make those on the other side hear of the Cause who had not heard of it while here? … A. Yes, surely sincere prayer always has its effect, and it has a great influence in the other word. We are never cut off from those who are there. The real and genuine influence is not in this world but in that other
selected.reason: Reported answer of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that sincere prayer influences the other world and that we are never cut off from those there; joins prayer and relationship.

selected.text: Know thou that he is with Us and abides in manifest spirit and delight. Were the veil to be lifted, the servants would behold him in an exalted station
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying a departed believer is with Him in spirit and delight and would be seen in an exalted station were the veil lifted; a brief assurance.

selected.text: Now, as the human spirit continues after death, it must either advance or decline, and in the next world to cease to advance is the same as to decline.

The heart of man is open to inspiration; this is spiritual communication. As in a dream one talks with a friend while the mouth is silent, so is it in the conversation of the spirit. A man may converse with the ego within him saying: "May I do this? Would it be advisable for me to do this work?" Such as this is conversation with the higher self
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: The spirit never leaves man even when he sleeps but it sees and knows. It never goes out and comes in again. It is the body that enters and makes its exit.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that the spirit never leaves man in sleep and that it is the body that enters and exits; a distinctive observation on the spirit and the body.

selected.text: make all aware of the station of death and what appeareth therefrom … By My life! In death are treasured God's consummate wisdom and His hidden mysteries
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh affirming that in death are treasured God’s consummate wisdom and His hidden mysteries; a brief statement of death’s meaning.

selected.text: This passing is not death and loss, nor extinction and nonexistence, but rather deliverance from the world of darkness and entrance into the eternal world.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá declaring that passing is not death, loss or extinction but deliverance into the eternal world; a clear consoling statement.

selected.text: I have made death a messenger of joy to thee. Wherefore dost thou grieve? I made the light to shed on thee its splendor. Why dost thou veil thyself therefrom?
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Make these friends alive and enduring in Your Kingdom, so that through Your grace and bounty they may become creators and players, singers and dancers
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayer that the friends may be alive in God’s Kingdom as creators, players, singers and dancers; supplies the music the closing why names.

selected.text: Grant then O my God, that Thy servant may consort with Thy chosen ones, Thy saints and Thy Messengers in heavenly places that the pen cannot tell nor the tongue recount
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Now she calls you from the Abha Kingdom: "O my children! If you knew what bounty I have attained, you would surely abandon the earthly body and soar to this divine realm."
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá giving the voice of a departed mother calling her children from the Abhá Kingdom about the bounty she has attained; a memorable family consolation.

selected.text: And though we are now scattered and dispersed, yearning and unsettled, ultimately we will be intimate companions and confidants in His shelter, harmonious and of one voice.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s assurance that though now scattered and yearning, the friends will at last be intimate companions in God’s shelter; a promise of reunion amid dispersion.

selected.text: and animal kingdoms, such a link may also exist between the material and the spiritual worlds after ascension. Know thou of a certainty that the soul is exalted above time and place and that the intervening link is also spiritual by nature, wholly detached from the contingent world
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá affirming that the soul is above time and place and that the link between the material and spiritual worlds after ascension is itself spiritual; qualifies talk of connection.

selected.text: he who hath ascended hath taken shelter beneath the canopies of the mercy of his Lord, and dwelleth in communion with God's chosen ones and trusted ones in an exalted Paradise
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh describing the one who has ascended as sheltered in his Lord’s mercy and in communion with God’s chosen ones; the promise that answers the acknowledged grief of separation.

selected.text: They have ascended to stations that no description can approach. In this case you must be joyful and carry out those things which after their ascension bring joy to their spirit
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh urging the bereaved to be joyful and to carry out what brings joy to the spirits of the departed; the practical link between remembrance and action.

selected.text: God hath forgiven him before his ascension and after his ascension. He hath caused him to enter a station the description of which the pens of all worlds are powerless to recount.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh assuring that God forgave a departed believer before and after his ascension and gave him an indescribable station; consolation through forgiveness.

selected.text: What is death but the transference of the soul from its nether abode to its exalted habitation. Through it the carpet of joy is rolled out and the standard of delight is unfurled
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh describing death as the transference of the soul to its exalted habitation, through which the carpet of joy is rolled out; a memorable image of welcome.

selected.text: Although those souls who hasten from this world of darkness to the luminous realm are sanctified from the conditions of the physical world and have no attachment to this mortal life
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá noting that souls who hasten to the luminous realm are sanctified from physical conditions; retained as the setting for the guide’s respect for the body that once held the spirit.

selected.text: That spirit can communicate with spirit is proven by the known fact of teaching … So soul can communicate with soul and in the realms of existence such intercommunication is possible
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that soul can communicate with soul, as shown by the fact of teaching; introduces spiritual communication.

selected.text: But concerning the spirit, know that thy pure son shall be with thee in the Kingdom of God and thou shalt witness his smiling face, illumined brow, handsome spirit and real happiness.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá promising a parent that their pure son will be with them in the Kingdom and that they will witness his smiling face; an intimate promise of recognition.

selected.text: This spiritual communication and mutual exchange of thoughts is conditioned upon certain facts that prepare the person in this world to communicate with the spirit of his departed ones.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that spiritual communication with the departed is conditioned on preparation in this world; a necessary qualification.

selected.text: In truth, those children are not lost, but rather hidden. For every thing hidden away there is another state of presence, and for every thing folded up there is another place of unfolding.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying that children who died are not lost but hidden, for every thing folded up has another place of unfolding; a memorable image of consolation.

selected.text: All blows fall upon the earthly body and elements of dust, not upon the pure soul. All harm reaches the garment of the body, not the spirit filled with spirit and the light of the gathering.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying that all blows fall on the earthly body and not on the pure soul; a brief consolation drawn from the distinction between body and spirit.

selected.text: Death and life are two gates for the manifestation of divine grace, bounty and mercy. Today is the day of bounty, mercy and generosity. Assuredly the sprinklings of the ocean of mercy shall embrace her
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh declaring that death and life are two gates for the manifestation of divine grace and mercy; a concise and memorable statement.

selected.text: His days were completed, his breath ceased, he cast off his garment and shed his raiment, returning unto Thee pure, sanctified, naked, sincere, aflame, attracted, yearning, and stirred by Thy fragrances.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayer describing a soul returning to God pure, sanctified, aflame and yearning when its days were completed; a vivid devotional portrait of death as return.

selected.text: We have sat together many times before, and we shall sit together many times again in the Kingdom. We shall laugh together very much in those times, and we shall tell of the things that befell us in the Path of God
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that we shall sit together again in the Kingdom, laugh together and tell of what befell us in the path of God; the guide’s closing hope of companionship.

selected.text: From this dark and constricted domain, he hath set out for a vast world imperceptible to the senses. He was earthly and became heavenly; he was of this evanescent world and he set foot in the divine world.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describing a departed believer who was earthly and became heavenly, setting out for a world imperceptible to the senses; a concise memorial.

selected.text: As many times as possible--at least once a year--you should make it a point to visit his tomb, for his spirit will be exhilarated through the loyalty of the friends, and in the world of God will it be happy.
selected.reason: Reported counsel of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá to visit a departed friend’s tomb at least once a year, since the spirit is gladdened by the loyalty of friends; a distinctive practical act of remembrance.

selected.text: So, when we leave here and go into the Kingdom of the Unseen, we shall know the use of the Bounties of God given us in this world. Here we are being prepared and given faculties which are for use in that world.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that we are being given faculties here whose use we shall know in the Kingdom of the Unseen; the clearest statement of preparation in this world.

selected.text: Do not think that you have lost both noble branches - God forbid! Rather, you will find them both as two trusts deposited with your Lord, under the protection of His care and providence and His grace and mercy.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá consoling a correspondent that two noble branches are not lost but are trusts deposited with their Lord; a distinctive image of consolation.

If you tried to explain to an embryo what this world is like could never understand -- but it understands when it is born, and its faculties can be used. So we cannot picture our state in the next world. All we know is that our consciousness, our personality, endures in some new state, and that that world is as much better than this one as this one is better than the dark womb of our mother was...

selected.reference: LG#700 (1st paragraph), LG#702 (last para.) (19 Jan. 1942 on behalf of Shoghi Effendi)
selected.text: Regarding your question concerning a deep and profound study of the teachings: of course the Baha'is can and should meditate upon the significances of the writings, and endeavour to grasp their meaning to the utmost.... However certain things are, by their very nature, a mystery to us, at least in our present stage of development. One of these is what the next world, the purely spiritual world, is like.         To try and visualize that realm in the terms of this physical one is absolutely impossible. 'Abdu'l-Baha has likened the relation of our souls in this world to our future life after death with the babe in its Mother's womb. All the faculties the infant is developing are, in the womb, absolutely useless to it. However, when it is born, it suddenly discovers their use, uses its eyes, its ears, hands, lungs, etc. in its new environment. Nor could the baby have possibly visualized its life after birth, while still unborn. So we cannot possibly understand or visualize what the condition and state of the future, purely spiritual, world is. To say it has time, space, and so on, is to delineate it by terms applicable to this material world and alien to that spiritual one.         The Guardian feels that, while there is no harm in speculation on these abstract matters, one should not attach too much importance to them. Science itself is far from having resolved the question of the nature of matter, and we cannot, in this physical world, grasp the spiritual one more than in a very fragmentary and inadequate manner.
